label: Sports game or competition

what_happens.title: What happens at the big game
goals: A game has a warm-up, playing time and an ending
Win or lose, the game ends with good game
what_happens.parentSkill: Walk through the order of the day: kit, warm-up, plan, play, breaks, good game.

who_is_there.title: Who is at the game
goals: The other team and the referee are part of the game
who_is_there.parentSkill: Tell your child you will be cheering, and that you love watching them play, whatever happens.

what_i_do.title: What I do in the game
goals: Warm up, listen, try the plan
Drink water and be a good sport
what_i_do.parentSkill: Agree on a "reset" move for after mistakes, like a deep breath and a clap.

if_scared.title: If I feel nervous
goals: Butterflies before a game are normal
Losing and mistakes feel bad and pass
Calm tools: breathing, a cue word, remembering the fun
if_scared.parentSkill: Name the nerves as energy: 'Butterflies mean your body is getting ready to play.'

rehearsal.title: Let's practise game day
goals: Practise the reset move and good game
Picture the game from warm-up to the end
rehearsal.parentSkill: Play a mini game at home and practise both winning and losing with good game.

steps: Put on the kit and pack a water bottle
Arrive and warm up with the coach and the team
Play the game, race or match
Take water breaks and cheer for teammates
Shake hands or say good game at the end
Talk about the best moment on the way home
sensory: a fast heartbeat and puffing breath
sweaty hands and a red face
the smell of grass or a gym floor
a team shirt with a number
honestyNotes: Kids may lose, make mistakes or not get much playing time; never promise winning. Praise effort, teamwork and courage, not the score. Nerves before a game are normal. Let the parent fill in the sport.

fallbackAnswer: Losing can feel sad, and that is okay.
[[GROWNUP]] is proud of you for playing, win or lose.

questionButtons.text: What if I make a mistake?
fallbackAnswer: Everyone makes mistakes, even big athletes.
Take a breath, clap once and keep going.
[[GROWNUP]] will tell you if they can come and where they will sit.
You can look for them and wave.
Coaches sometimes shout so players can hear on a big field.
Loud does not mean angry, and you can ask the coach what they meant.
Bumps can happen in sports. Tell the coach straight away.
The coach knows what to do, and you can take a break.

questionButtons.text: What if I don't get to play much?
fallbackAnswer: Coaches share playing time over many games.
Cheering from the bench helps the team too.
Butterflies mean your body is getting ready to play.
Slow breaths help them settle.

questionButtons.text: What if I forget the rules?
fallbackAnswer: Coaches and teammates will remind you.
The referee helps everyone follow the rules too.

questionButtons.text: What if the crowd is loud?
fallbackAnswer: Crowds cheer and whistles blow, and it can be loud.
You can focus on the ball and your teammates.

questionButtons.text: How should I act if we win?
fallbackAnswer: Celebrate with your team, then say good game to the other team.
Winning kindly is part of being a good sport.

techniques.label: A reset move
techniques.how: After a mistake: one breath, one clap, and say next.

techniques.label: An effort goal
techniques.how: Pick a goal that does not depend on winning, like passing to friends.

techniques.label: Cheering for teammates
techniques.how: Cheer and clap for teammates, even from the bench.

techniques.label: Saying good game
techniques.how: Practise good game for winning and for losing.

techniques.label: A pre-game song
techniques.how: Pick a song to hum during warm-up.

techniques.label: Telling the coach
techniques.how: Tell the coach about any hurt or worry.

techniques.label: A wave from the side
techniques.how: Agree a wave or thumbs up between you and your child.

techniques.label: Smell the flower, blow the candle
techniques.how: Breathe in slowly through the nose and out like blowing a candle.

pain: If something hurts, tell your coach and take a break.
body: Butterflies mean your body is getting ready.
sensory: The crowd is loud. Watch the ball.
Your heart beats fast when you run. That is normal.
strangers: The coach is there to help the team.
The referee keeps the game fair.

social: Being a good teammate matters most.

Before bed, here is a story about a young rabbit called Rue.
Rue was on the Meadow Hoppers team.
On game day, Rue put on a green shirt with the number seven.
First the team warmed up, hop, hop, stretch.
Then Coach Heron said, pass the ball and help each other.
Next the whistle blew, peep, and the game began.
Rue ran and passed and missed and ran again.
At half time, everyone drank water in the shade.
The other team scored one more goal than the Hoppers.
At the end, Rue said, good game, to every player.
Tomorrow evening, the story goes on.
After that, the game starts with a whistle.
There are breaks for water and a rest.
Some games are won, and some are lost.
Last, everyone says good game and shakes hands.

That is the body getting ready to play.

What if I miss, what if we lose, Rue thought.
Mama Rabbit did not say, you will win.
Mama said, you might miss, and you might lose, and I will be proud of you.
Butterflies mean your body is getting ready.

Rue felt sad, and Mama gave a big hug.

Competitions follow rules so every team has a fair chance, and a referee or judge makes the calls.
Warm-ups prepare muscles and the heart, which helps prevent injuries.
Coaches plan positions and rotations, so playing time is shared over a season.
Even professional athletes lose often; what they practise is coming back after mistakes.
[[CHILD]] can set one personal goal for the game that does not depend on the score.
The referee's job is to keep the game fair and safe, even when a call feels wrong.
Respecting the other team is part of the sport; without them, there is no game.
Coaches notice effort and attitude as much as skill.
Supporting a teammate who made a mistake builds trust on a team.
[[CHILD]] can thank the coach and the referee after the game.
Athletes use reset routines because the brain replays mistakes; a breath and a cue word help it move on.
Focusing on the next play, not the last one, is a skill that improves with practice.
Hydration affects energy and concentration more than most players realise.
Good sportsmanship includes winning politely, not only losing well.
[[CHILD]] can pick a cue word, like next, to say after a mistake.
Pre-game nerves are adrenaline, the same chemical that helps muscles react faster.
Calling the feeling excited instead of scared can actually help performance.
Feeling upset after a loss shows you care; it usually fades within a few hours.
If [[CHILD]] does not want to talk right after a game, that is fine, and a snack and quiet often help.
[[CHILD]] can write down one thing that went well after each game.
Visualisation, picturing the game in detail, is a technique real athletes use.
Sleep, a good meal and water the day before matter for energy.
A small pre-game routine, like a song or a stretch, signals the brain it is time to focus.
Setting effort goals, like hustling back on defence, keeps motivation high whatever the score.
[[CHILD]] can choose the pre-game song.
